hook: A bat and ball cost 1.10. Your gut already has an answer. Check it.
title: Fast & Slow Thinking

game.question: A bat and a ball cost 1.10 together. The bat costs 1.00 more than the ball. How much is the ball, in cents?
game.explain: If the ball were 10, the bat would be 1.10 and the total 1.20. Ball 0.05 + bat 1.05 = 1.10. Most people's first answer is 10, including many students at top universities.

insight: The 10-cent answer arrives instantly and feels right. That's your fast mind. The slow mind only checks when you ask it to. Clever people miss this too; a pause is what helps.
model: Fast thinking proposes, slow thinking checks. When it feels obvious and matters, check once.
try_today: Say your gut answer out loud before your next decision that matters, then ask: 'How would I check this?'

source.work: Cognitive Reflection and Decision Making (2005); Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011)

try_team: Give everyone the bat-and-ball puzzle on paper, answers written silently. Reveal, then ask: which of our choices feel this obvious but never get checked?

hook: Hare or owl: who's actually making your decisions this week?
title: Who's Driving: Hare or Owl?

questions.q: A message annoys you. You usually…
Buying something pricey (a phone, shoes, a gadget), you…
When a headline makes you angry, you…

options.label: Work it out step by step

zones.label: Hare-led
zones.text: Today your answers lean fast. That's efficient for routine stuff. For the few choices that matter, add one deliberate pause.

zones.label: Shared driving
zones.text: Today your answers switch between speeds. The skill now is noticing which moments deserve the owl.

zones.label: Owl-led
zones.text: Today your answers lean slow. Great for big calls. Watch for overthinking small, reversible ones; the hare handles those well.

insight: Neither speed is better. The fast mind slips on numbers, anger and new things. 'System 1 and 2' (Stanovich & West, 2000) is a metaphor, not two brain parts.
model: Let the hare handle the routine; call the owl for anything costly, emotional, or new.
try_today: Pick one trigger (an angry message, a pricey purchase) and make it your rule to wait 10 minutes first.
try_team: Agree on one shared 'owl rule', e.g. nobody replies to a heated group message for 10 minutes. Check in after a week: did it help?

hook: We'll show you a random number first. Watch it bend your guess.
title: Anchoring

game.question: What percentage of UN member countries are in Africa?
game.explain: 54 of the 193 UN members are African: about 28%. You saw 65 first. If your guess landed above 35%, that number probably pulled you up. In the 1974 study, people who saw a wheel land on 65 guessed a median of 45%; those who saw 10 guessed 25%.

insight: An irrelevant number still drags your guess toward it. Price tags like 'was 199, now 99' use this. Knowing about it helps a little; bringing your own number helps more.
model: The first number sets the field. Bring your own number before you hear theirs.
try_today: Before your next salary talk, quote or haggle, write your own number and one reason it's fair, before you hear theirs.

source.work: Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (1974)

try_team: Before any group estimate (trip cost, deadline, budget), everyone writes a number privately, then reveal together. No one anchors the room.

hook: Your brain ranks dangers by how easily they come to mind. Test it.
title: Availability Bias

game.prompt: Compared to how often it feels like it happens…

items.why: Crashes get huge coverage. Per mile, commercial flying is far safer than driving.
Worldwide, unprovoked shark deaths are usually in single digits per year.

items.text: Older adults dying after a fall
items.why: Falls are a leading cause of injury death for people over 65. Quiet, rarely in the news.

items.text: A child taken by a total stranger
items.why: Stranger abductions are very rare; most missing children are runaways or family cases.

items.text: Heart disease as a cause of death
items.why: It's the top cause of death worldwide (WHO), yet rarely makes headlines.
About 1.2 million road deaths a year worldwide (WHO). So routine they're barely news.

insight: Vivid, recent, dramatic events are easy to recall, so they feel common. Slow, ordinary risks hide. Your feed is a highlight reel of rare events, not a map of risk.
model: Easy to imagine is not the same as likely. Ask for the count, not the story.
try_today: Look up one number the next time a scary story grabs you: how many times a year does this actually happen?

source.work: Availability: A Heuristic for Judging Frequency and Probability (1973)

try_team: Everyone names the danger they worry about most. Look up one real yearly number for each together. Which fears shrink, and which grow?

hook: 2, 4, 6 follows a secret rule. Most people's first guess is wrong.
title: Confirmation Bias

steps.scenario: The numbers 2-4-6 follow a hidden rule. You can test any three numbers and learn if they fit. Your hunch: 'even numbers going up by 2.' Which test teaches you the most?

options.feedback: It fits, but it would fit your hunch either way. You'd learn nothing new. This is what most people try.
Another yes, but again only a test your hunch already predicts. Confirming feels productive; it rarely is.
Yes! Your hunch says 'no'. If it fits, your hunch is wrong. That's a real test. Spoiler: it fits.

options.text: Just guess the rule now
options.feedback: Bold! But without a test that could prove you wrong, you'd be guessing blind.

steps.scenario: 1-2-3 fits. So does 3-17-90. 6-4-2 does not. What's the rule?

options.text: Any three numbers going up
options.feedback: Correct. In Wason's 1960 study, only about 1 in 5 people named it on their first try, mostly because they only tested examples they expected to fit.

options.text: Numbers with a pattern
options.feedback: Close in spirit, but 3-17-90 has no neat pattern. Simpler: they just go up.

options.text: Even numbers only
options.feedback: 1-2-3 fit, so odd numbers are allowed. The rule is broader: any rising sequence.

insight: We often test ideas in ways that can only say 'yes'. It feels like proof but isn't. Researchers debate how irrational this is; the fix is clear: seek what could prove you wrong.
model: Don't ask 'what fits my idea?' Ask 'what would I see if I were wrong?'
try_today: Pick one belief you hold firmly. Write down one thing that, if you saw it, would change your mind. Go look for it.

source.work: On the failure to eliminate hypotheses in a conceptual task (1960)

try_team: Play 2-4-6: one person holds a secret rule, others test triples aloud. Afterwards count how many tests could have gotten a 'no'.

from_source.quote: The human understanding when it has once adopted an opinion ... draws all things else to support and agree with it.
from_source.cite: Francis Bacon, Novum Organum (1620), Book I, Aphorism 46 (trans. Spedding, Ellis & Heath)
from_source.next_read: Novum Organum, Book I, Aphorisms 45–52 (the 'Idols of the Tribe')

hook: In an argument, are you defending a fort or drawing a map?
title: Soldier or Scout?

questions.q: Someone shares a study that disagrees with you. First thought:

options.label: Look for what's wrong with it, but not what's right
Check its methods, the same way I'd check one I agreed with
Read what they found before judging

questions.q: When did you last change your mind on something you cared about?
Your feed mostly shows people who…

options.label: I follow some smart critics on purpose

zones.label: Soldier mode
zones.text: Today's answers lean toward defending, which is very human. Try treating one belief as a draft, not a fort.

zones.label: Switching
zones.text: Today's answers mix scouting and defending. Notice which topics made you defensive; that's where your map is least checked.

zones.label: Scout mode
zones.text: Today's answers lean curious about being wrong. Keep it kind: scouts share maps, they don't sneer at others' wrong turns.

insight: Everyone slips into defending. Scouting isn't caring less; it's wanting an accurate map more than wanting to be right. Your answers are a snapshot, not a verdict.
model: A soldier asks 'Can I believe this?' or 'Must I believe this?' A scout asks 'Is it true?'
try_today: In your next disagreement, ask one honest question: 'What would change your mind?' Then answer it yourself too.
try_team: In your next group debate, each side must state the other side's best argument first, until the other side says 'yes, that's it'.

hook: Heads you win 150, tails you lose 100. Do you flip?
title: Loss Aversion

game.prompt: One fair coin flip, real money in your own currency. Heads: you win 150. Tails: you lose 100. On average this bet pays you 25. Do you take it?
game.reveal: No wrong answer here: it's your money. But notice the pull. In Kahneman's studies most people refuse, wanting a win of about 200 before risking 100. Losses tend to feel roughly 1.5–2.5× as strong as equal gains.

insight: Saying no is fine when the loss would really hurt. But we often skip small, smart risks just because losing stings. Some research finds the effect smaller than claimed for small amounts.
model: Losses shout, gains whisper. For small, repeatable bets, judge the average, not the sting.
try_today: Name one small risk you've avoided (asking, applying, trying). Write the realistic worst case. Is it really that bad?

source.work: Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk (1979)

try_team: Each person writes one small risk they've avoided. Swap papers and estimate the realistic worst case for each other. Is it as bad as it felt?

from_source.quote: We suffer more ... when we fall from a better to a worse situation, than we ever enjoy when we rise ...
from_source.cite: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759), Part VI, Section I
from_source.next_read: The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Part VI, Section I, 'Of the Character of the Individual, so far as it affects his own Happiness'

hook: Same mug, same room. Owning it for 5 minutes changes its price.
title: The Endowment Effect

game.question: Students got a free mug. Those who got one named a selling price; those who didn't named a buying price. How many times more did owners want?
game.explain: About 2.5×. In Kahneman, Knetsch & Thaler's 1990 study, owners asked a median of about $7.12 and buyers offered about $2.87. Same mug. Owning it for 5 minutes made giving it up feel like a loss.

insight: Owning something makes letting go feel like losing, so we overprice our stuff. The effect is real but its size depends on the setup; some studies find it much smaller.
model: Ask 'Would I buy this today, at this price?' not 'How much would losing it hurt?'
try_today: Look at one thing you're selling online or keeping in your wardrobe or garage: would you buy it today at that price?
try_team: Ask everyone: name one thing we keep only because we already have it (a tool, a habit, a club, a routine). Would we choose it again today?

source.work: Experimental Tests of the Endowment Effect and the Coase Theorem (1990); Plott & Zeiler (2005)

hook: Stuck on how to succeed? Ask how you'd fail instead.
title: Inversion

steps.scenario: Your goal: be a better friend this year. Which question gets you a useful answer fastest?

options.text: How could I be the perfect friend?
options.feedback: Nice aim, but 'perfect' gives vague answers like 'be there more'. Hard to act on.

options.text: What would make sure I lose my friends?
options.feedback: Yes. Failure is easy to picture: cancel last minute, only talk about me, forget birthdays. Concrete and fixable.

options.text: What do the experts say friendship is?
options.feedback: Useful later, but it's about friendship in general, not your habits. Inversion goes straight to yours.

steps.scenario: Your list: cancel last minute, only talk about yourself, never ask questions, forget birthdays. Best next move?

options.text: Fix all four starting tomorrow
options.feedback: Big energy! But four changes at once rarely stick. Start with one.

options.text: Circle the one you already do a little, and stop it this week
options.feedback: Exactly. Small, honest, doable. Removing one quiet mistake often beats adding a big new effort.

options.text: Feel bad about the list
options.feedback: Very human, but guilt doesn't change much. The list is a map, not a verdict. Pick one item.

insight: Your brain spots ways to fail faster than recipes for success. Mathematician Carl Jacobi advised 'invert, always invert'; investor Charlie Munger made it a life habit.
model: Ask what would guarantee failure, then don't do that.
try_today: Pick one goal. Write 3 ways to guarantee it fails. Circle the one you're closest to doing, and drop it today.
try_team: Ask the group: 'How could we make this trip, project or term a total disaster?' List ideas for 5 minutes, then pick one to prevent.

from_source.cite: Carl Jacobi, as quoted by Charlie Munger, Harvard School commencement speech (1986)
from_source.next_read: Charlie Munger's 1986 Harvard School commencement speech on prescriptions for misery, reprinted in Poor Charlie's Almanack

hook: A city paid people for every dead cobra. Guess what it got more of.
title: Second-Order Thinking

steps.scenario: Colonial Delhi, as the classic story goes. Cobras are a danger, so officials pay a reward for every dead cobra handed in. What happens next?

options.text: The cobra problem shrinks
options.feedback: That's the first-order guess, and it's what officials expected. The story has a twist.

options.text: People start breeding cobras to cash in
options.feedback: Yes. In the story, people farmed cobras for the reward. When officials scrapped it, breeders let the snakes go: more cobras than before.

options.text: Nobody bothers to hunt cobras
options.feedback: The opposite. Plenty of dead cobras came in, just not in the way that helped.

steps.scenario: A parent wants their kid to read more, so they plan to pay a coin for every book finished. Ask 'and then what?' twice. Best tweak?

options.text: Pay more per book
options.feedback: More pressure on the same number. Expect thinner books and skimming: the count goes up, the reading may not.

options.text: Read and chat about books together, and celebrate finishing a hard one
options.feedback: Good. You reward the real goal (enjoying and understanding) and keep a human check, so gaming it is harder.

options.text: Never reward anything
options.feedback: Understandable after the cobras! But rewards can work; just ask what the number will make people do.

insight: First-order asks 'what now?' Second-order asks 'and then what?' Rewards shift behavior in unplanned ways. The cobra tale is a parable with thin records; Horst Siebert named the effect after it.
model: Every fix creates new incentives. Ask 'and then what?' at least twice.
try_today: Write 'and then what?' before your next rule, rule-change, or reward (for you, your kids, or a group), and answer it twice.

source.work: The Most Important Thing (2011); Der Kobra-Effekt (2001)

try_team: Before rewarding a number (bugs fixed, sales calls, chores done), ask together: 'How could someone hit this number without helping?' Then adjust.

from_source.quote: We can never do merely one thing.
from_source.cite: Garrett Hardin, 'The Cybernetics of Competition', Perspectives in Biology and Medicine (1963)
from_source.next_read: Frédéric Bastiat, That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen (1850), Chapter 1, 'The Broken Window' (public domain)

hook: A test says you have a rare condition. How worried should you be?
title: Base Rates

game.question: A condition affects 1 in 1,000 people. A test catches every real case but gives a false positive to 5% of healthy people. You test positive. Chance you have it?
game.explain: Of 1,000 people: 1 truly has it. About 50 healthy people also test positive. So 1 of ~51 positives is real: about 2%. In a 1978 Harvard study, 27 of 60 doctors and students answered 95%; only 11 got about 2%.

insight: When something is rare, most positives are false alarms. That's why doctors confirm with a second test. This is just the math; real results need a real doctor.
model: Start with how common it is, then adjust for the new evidence. Rare things stay fairly rare.
try_today: Ask 'Out of 1,000 similar cases, how many usually turn out this way?' the next time a story or alarm surprises you.

source.work: Interpretation by Physicians of Clinical Laboratory Results (1978)

try_team: Turn one scary claim into counts together: 'Out of 1,000 people like this, how many…?' Sketch the 1,000 as dots if it helps.

from_source.quote: A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence.
from_source.cite: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), Section X, Part I
from_source.next_read: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X, 'Of Miracles', Part I

hook: One sentence about a stranger. Your gut picks a job in a second.
title: The Count Beats the Story

game.prompt: Steve is a man in the USA. He's shy, tidy, loves order and small details, and is happiest with a quiet book. Is Steve more likely a librarian or a farmer?
game.reveal: Librarian is the natural pick: the story fits. But Kahneman notes the US had over 20 male farmers for every male librarian. Even if Steve fits librarians far better, farmers still win on the count.

insight: A vivid description makes us forget how common each option is. Kahneman and Tversky showed this in 1973. Thinking in counts ('out of 100 men like Steve…') makes the error shrink.
model: The story says who fits. The count says who's likely. Ask the count first.
try_today: Next time you judge someone or something from one detail, ask: 'How common is each option in general?' before you decide.
try_team: Before judging a new idea, person or rumour from one story, ask the group: 'How often does this usually happen?' Find one real number together.

source.work: On the Psychology of Prediction (1973); Judgment under Uncertainty (1974); Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011), Introduction; Gigerenzer & Hoffrage (1995)

hook: You watched for one minute. You're already sure who's smarter.
title: The Quizmaster Illusion

game.prompt: A coin toss splits two people. One writes 10 hard trivia questions from their own odd knowledge. The other must answer them and gets about 4 right. Who seems more knowledgeable?
choices: Can't tell: the coin set the roles
game.reveal: The coin decided it. Asking your own questions is easy; answering someone else's is hard. Yet in Ross's 1977 study, watchers rated the questioner more knowledgeable, and so did the people answering.

insight: We see the person, not the setup that made them look good or bad. Even knowing the roles were random didn't stop the bias.
model: Before judging the player, look at the role they were handed.
try_today: Next time someone looks clueless (a new classmate, colleague or relative), ask: 'Whose home turf is this?' before you judge them.
try_team: Swap roles for 5 minutes: the newest person explains their own speciality and the expert asks questions. Notice who suddenly looks 'smart'.

source.work: Social Roles, Social Control, and Biases in Social-Perception Processes (1977)

hook: Someone lets you down. Your brain writes their whole biography.
title: Blaming People, Not Situations

steps.scenario: Your group project partner hasn't sent their part, and it's due tomorrow. Your first thought should be…

options.text: 'They're lazy. Typical.'
options.feedback: Understandable when you're stressed, but it's a guess about character from one moment. You don't yet know what's going on for them.

options.text: 'Something's probably in the way. I'll ask what's up and what they still need.'
options.feedback: Best pick. You stay open to the situation (illness, a shift at work, a crashed laptop) and you still chase the deadline.

options.text: 'Not my problem. I'll just do it all myself.'
options.feedback: It fixes tonight but skips finding out why. If the cause is fixable, it'll happen again.

steps.scenario: A usually reliable team member has missed two deadlines this month. As their manager, you…

options.text: Note it in their review as a commitment problem.
options.feedback: That locks in a character story before checking the setup. Two slips in a steady record often point to workload, unclear priorities or something at home.

options.text: Ask privately what changed and what's competing for their time.
options.feedback: Best pick. Look at the situation first: shifting priorities and overload often explain a sudden change better than 'they stopped caring'.

options.text: Say nothing and hope it sorts itself out.
options.feedback: Kind, but silence leaves both of you guessing. A curious question is kinder than a quiet verdict.

steps.scenario: Your grown-up son forgot to call on your birthday. Before you pick up the phone, you tell yourself…

options.text: 'He doesn't care about me anymore.'
options.feedback: A painful leap from one missed call. That turns a busy day into a story about the whole relationship.

options.text: 'His week must be chaotic. I'll call and see how he is.'
options.feedback: Best pick. A hectic job, a sick child or simple overload can explain a missed call. Calling keeps the door open either way.

options.text: 'I'll wait and see how long it takes him.'
options.feedback: A waiting game usually lets the hurt grow. A warm call answers the question faster.

insight: Situations explain more than we think: in a 1973 study, hurried trainee ministers rarely stopped for a man slumped in a doorway. The flip side (excusing ourselves) is weaker than once claimed.
model: Others' slips: ask 'what's in their way?' before 'what's wrong with them?'
try_today: The next time someone annoys you, name two situations that could explain it before you decide what they're like.
try_team: Take one recent mistake. Everyone lists three situation causes (time, information, tools) before anyone names a person. Fix one cause.

source.work: The Intuitive Psychologist and His Shortcomings (Ross, 1977); From Jerusalem to Jericho (Darley & Batson, 1973); The Actor-Observer Asymmetry in Attribution: A (Surprising) Meta-Analysis (Malle, 2006)
